column2: As the two watched, the lifter of the Bhargava line vanished, king of kings; then the king fell to the ground.
Having recovered a moment with Sahadevi, the greatly radiant one made supreme effort again to search for him.
[Bhishma said:] Not seeing that sage, the king with his wife, wearied, turned back, ashamed and with his senses lost.
Entering the city, wretched, he said nothing, thinking only of Chyavana's conduct.
Then with an empty mind the king entered his house and saw the descendant of Bhrigu lying on that bed.
Astonished, the two, thinking on that wonder, became rested by the sight of the sage.
Standing in their places, they massaged him again; then the great sage slept on the other side.
In the same time the mighty one awoke, and the two, fearful, made no change.
Awakened, the sage said to them, lord of men, "Let me be given an oil massage; I shall bathe," Bharata.
Saying "So be it," the two, hungry and worn with toil, attended him with very costly oil cooked a hundred times.
When Bhargava saw the two unchanged, he rose suddenly and entered the bathing room, where a bath fit for a king was prepared.
Disregarding all that, he vanished right there; the sage again vanished as the king looked on, and the couple did not show anger, bull of the Bharatas.
Then the blessed lord, the descendant of Bhrigu, bathed and seated on a lion throne, showed himself to Kushika and his wife.
With glad face, the king Kushika and his wife, bowing, unchanged, reported "The food is ready."
Let it be brought, the sage said to the king; and the king brought that food with his wife.
Many kinds of meat dishes, various vegetables, vesavara preparations and light drinks,
rasala, apupas, varied modakas, shadava juices of many kinds, and forest food, the sage's meal,
wonderful fruits and much food to be eaten, jujubes, ingudi, kashmari, bhallataka and banyan fruits,
whatever householders eat and whatever forest-dwellers eat, the king brought all, from fear of the sage's curse.
Then all that was set before Chyavana; and the sage, having brought together all that and the bed and seat,
covered them with lovely garments along with the eating utensils, and Chyavana, Bhrigu's descendant, set it all on fire.
The couple of great vows showed no anger; as they looked on, he vanished again.
The royal sage stayed right there that night with his wife, silent and glorious, and no anger entered him.
Food of many kinds, always prepared in the king's house, choice beds and abundant ablutions,
and garments of various kinds, were obtained; and Chyavana then could not find an opening.
Again the brahmana sage said to King Kushika, "Quickly carry me with your wife in a chariot where I tell you."
So be it, said the king, unhesitating, to the ascetic; "Blessed one, shall it be a pleasure chariot or a war chariot?"
Thus addressed by the glad king, Chyavana replied gladly to the conqueror of enemy cities:

Prepare quickly that chariot of yours which is held for battle, with weapons, banner, spear, lances and staff,
mahabharata:13:53.30	resounding with a hundred small bells, joined with javelins, bound with maces and swords, and with a hundred of the best.
Saying "So be it," he prepared the great chariot, placing his wife at the left pole and himself at the right.
He took a three-pointed goad with a diamond tip; having given all this, the king then said:
Blessed one, where shall the chariot go? Let the descendant of Bhrigu say; where you tell, brahmana sage, there your chariot will go.
Thus asked, the blessed one replied to the king: "From now it must go step by step, slowly.
Let there be no strain on me; go as I please, happy; I am to be carried, and let all people see.
No traveller is to be driven off; to them I shall give wealth, and to the brahmanas who ask me for wishes on the road.
I shall give all wealth and jewels without remainder; let it be done wholly, king; do not hesitate."
Hearing his words, the king said to his servants, "Whatever the sage says, all that is to be given without suspicion."
Then many jewels, women, carriages, goats and sheep, gold worked and unworked, and elephants like mountains
followed the sage, and the king's ministers on all sides, and all that city was full of cries of alarm.
The two, urged suddenly by the sharp-tipped goad, struck on the back and hips, unchanged, drew him.
Trembling, without food, wasted by fifty nights, the two heroic spouses drew that best chariot with difficulty.
Struck much and badly, bleeding from the wounds, great king, the two looked like flowering kimshuka trees.
Seeing them, the townspeople, much given to grief, afraid of a curse, said nothing.
They all said to each other, "See the strength of austerity; though angry we cannot even look at the best of sages.
Ah, the might of the blessed great sage of purified self; and see what steadiness the king and his wife have.
Though tired, they draw this chariot with hardship; and the descendant of Bhrigu saw no change in them."
[Bhishma said:] Then, seeing the two unchanged, the lifter of Bhrigu's line distributed wealth as Vaishravana does.
There too the glad king did as commanded; then the blessed best of sages was pleased with him.
Getting down from the best chariot, he released the couple, and having duly freed them, he then spoke.
With a soft, deep and very clear voice Bhargava said: "I give you a boon, the best; say it, Bharata."
The wise best of sages touched the delicate pair with his hands, like nectar, out of affection, best of the Bharatas.
Then the king said: "We have no weariness here; we are rested by your power and meditation alone, Bhargava."
Then the blessed Chyavana, very glad, said to them: "What I said before is not in vain; it will be.
This is a lovely place, the bank of the Ganga; for some time I shall live here, intent on my vow, lord of the earth.
Go to your own city, son; when rested you will come again; tomorrow, lord of men, you will see me here with your wife.
You must have no anger; the good has come to you; whatever you desire in your heart will all come to be."
Thus addressed, Kushika, with a delighted inner self, said to the tiger among sages these meaningful words:

I have no anger, greatly fortunate one; I am purified by you, blessed one; we two are become young, beautiful and strong.
mahabharata:13:53.60	The wounds made on me and my wife by the goad and whip I do not see on our bodies; I am well with my wife.
mahabharata:13:53.61	And I see this queen, sage, like a divine apsara, joined with supreme beauty, as I saw her before.
mahabharata:13:53.62	By your grace all this has come about, great sage; this is no wonder in you, blessed one of true prowess.
Thus addressed, he replied to Kushika: "Come here again with your wife, lord of men."
Thus addressed and permitted, the royal sage, bowing to him, went, joined with his new body, to the city like the lord of gods.
Then ministers with priests, the army, courtesans and all the subjects came to him.
Surrounded by them, King Kushika, blazing with supreme glory, entered the city glad, honoured by bards.
Then, entering the city and doing the rites of the whole day, the king ate and passed the night with his wife.
Then the two, seeing each other's new youth, as if the two immortals free of old age, rejoiced lying in bed, embodied, joined with beauty given by the boon of the brahmana.
And the sage too, increaser of the glory of Bhrigu's line, the ascetic, by his wisdom created a lovely prosperous forest adorned with jewels of many kinds, such as Shatakratu has not.
Then the king saw a palace wholly of gold, rich in thousands of jewelled pillars, like a city of the gandharvas; there Kushika saw divine wonders.
He saw mountains with lovely peaks, lotus ponds with lotuses, and various picture halls and gateways, Bharata, and ground covered with grass and a floor of gold.
Mangoes in bloom, ketaka and uddalaka, dhava, ashoka, muchukunda and flowering atimuktaka,
champaka, tilaka, bhavya, jackfruit, vanjula and flowering karnikara were seen there and here.
The king saw dark creepers, varanapushpi and ashtapadika set here and there.
Trees bearing lotuses and water lilies, flowers of all seasons, celestial cars and palaces like lotuses.
Cool waters and somewhere hot, Bharata; varied seats and excellent beds.
Couches wholly of gold, spread with costly coverings, and endless food and drink were provided here and there.
On every side he saw very charming sounds, in places troops of apsarases and gandharvas, king.
He saw others embraced by their beloved there; and he did not see them, and the king saw them again.
The king heard there very sweet singing and the sound of recitation, and very sweet swans.
Seeing that exceeding wonder, the king thought in mind: "Is this a dream, a confusion of mind, or truth indeed?
Ah, have I with this body reached the highest goal, the holy Uttara Kurus, or Amaravati?
What is this great wonder I see?" So he thought; and while thinking so he saw the best of sages,
lying in that golden car, crowded with jewelled pillars, on a costly divine bed, the descendant of Bhrigu.
The king with his wife went to him with great joy; then Chyavana vanished again, and that bed.
Then he saw him again in another part of the forest, seated on a kusha mat, muttering, of great vows; thus by the power of yoga the brahmana bewildered the king.
In a moment that forest, those troops of apsarases, the gandharvas and trees all vanished.
And the bank of the Ganga became silent again, king, and was full of kusha grass and anthills as before.
Then King Kushika with his wife came to supreme wonder at that deed, seeing that great marvel.
Then Kushika, full of joy, said to his wife: "See, good one, how wonderful, hard to see feelings have been seen.
By the grace of the chief of Bhrigus, what else is there except the power of austerity? By austerity is gained what cannot be by wishes.
Austerity is better even than rule over the three worlds; for the ascetic plays with well-heated austerity.
Ah, the power of the Brahmarishi, the great-souled Chyavana; if he wished he could create other worlds by his austerity's might.
Brahmanas alone would be born, of holy speech, intellect and deed; who else here would dare to do it except Chyavana?
Brahminhood is hard to get in the world; kingship is easy for men; by the power of brahminhood we two were yoked to the chariot as to a pole.
Thinking so, he was known to Chyavana, who looking at him said to the king, "Come quickly."
Thus addressed, he went with his wife to the great sage, and the king bowed to him who is to be saluted with the head.
Having bestowed blessings on him, the sage said to the lord of men, the wise one, soothing the bull among men: "Sit."
Then Bhargava, restored to his nature, spoke to the king in gentle speech, as if satisfying him, Bharata:

King, you have rightly conquered here the five in the five, the senses with mind as sixth; therefore you are freed from hardship.
mahabharata:13:54.35	You have rightly served me, son, best of speakers; there is in you not even the least subtle wrong.
mahabharata:13:54.36	Give me leave, king, I shall go as I came; I am pleased with you, king of kings; accept a boon.
[Kushika said:] "Standing in the midst of fire, blessed one, in your presence, I have lived, tiger of Bhrigus; that I was not burnt is much.
This is the chief boon I have got, descendant of Bhrigu, that you are pleased with our conduct, and my family is purified, sinless one.
This is my favour, brahmana, and the purpose of life; this is the fruit of kingship and my highest austerity.
But if you are pleased with me, descendant of Bhrigu, I have a certain doubt; you ought to tell it to me."
[Kushika said:] "If you are pleased, blessed one, Bhargava, tell me; I wish to hear the reason for your living in my house,
sleeping on one side for twenty-one days, going out without saying anything, bull among sages,
suddenly vanishing and again appearing, and again sleeping twenty-one days, brahmana,
going anointed with oil, eating in my house, the food of many kinds brought to you that was burnt by the fire, and the sudden departure by chariot done by you,
the giving away of wealth, the sight of the forest, great sage, and of many golden palaces,
the sight of couches with feet of jewels and coral, and again his disappearance: I wish to hear the reason.
I am exceedingly bewildered by this, thinking day and night, and I find no settlement of all this. I wish to hear the truth of it in full, ascetic."
[Chyavana said:] "Hear all of it without remainder, what this is and by what cause; being asked so, king, it cannot be left untold.
By the conflict of brahmin and kshatriya there will be a mixing of the line; your grandson will be born, king, endowed with splendour and prowess.
Then, to guard my own family, I came to you, wishing to cut off the Kushikas and burn your family.
Then, coming to you, lord of the earth, I said, 'I shall undertake a certain rule; let service be done.'
I found no misdeed of yours in the house, therefore you live, royal sage; it would not be otherwise.
Taking this resolve, I slept twenty-one days: 'If anyone should wake me,' lord of men.
When you and your wife, touched, did not wake me, then I was pleased with you in mind, best of kings.
I rose and went out: if you had asked me 'Where will you go?', I would have cursed you, lord.
And I vanished again and again in your house, lying in yoga for twenty-one days.
'Hungry, he might find fault with me, or from fatigue,' lord of men; taking this resolve, I made you two lean with hunger.
No anger even slight arose in your mind, lord of men, nor in your wife's, best of men; therefore I am pleased with you.
I burned the food that I had had brought, 'if you were to be angry from envy'; and that you bore.
Then, mounting the chariot, I said to you, lord of men, 'Carry me with your wife,' and you did so.
You were without suspicion, lord of men, and I was pleased with that; and even in the giving away of wealth, anger did not assail you.
Then, pleased with you, king, this was done again by me, the forest for you and your wife, know that, lord of men.
For your pleasure this sight of heaven was made by me, that you saw in this forest, king, a divine illustration.
A glimpse of heaven was experienced by you, king, with this body, for a moment, with your wife, best of kings.
For illustration of austerity and dharma, lord of men, the longing you had there was also known to me.
You wish for brahminhood and austerity, lord of the earth, scorning kingship and lordship of the gods.
It is as you say, dear one: brahminhood is hard to get; being a brahmana, sagehood, and in sagehood, asceticism.
This wish of yours will be fulfilled: from Kushika will come a Kaushika, twice-born; reaching the third person, brahminhood will come.
Your line, best of kings, will be by the splendour of Bhrigus alone; your grandson will be a brahmana, an ascetic, bright as fire.
He will cause fear to gods and men and to all three worlds; I tell you this truth.
Choose a boon, royal sage, what is in your mind; I shall go on pilgrimage; time is passing."

[Kushika said:] "This is the boon I have today, that you are pleased, great sage; let it be as you say, that austerity be in my grandson, sinless one, and let brahminhood be for my family, blessed one; this is my boon.
And I wish to hear again at length, blessed one, how brahminhood will come to my family, descendant of Bhrigu; who will be that kinsman of mine, and who also approved?"
[Chyavana said:] "The kshatriyas are always the sacrificers of the Bhrigus, lord of men, and they will go to division by a cause joined with fate.
And the kshatriyas, lord of men, will kill all the Bhrigus, cutting even the embryos, afflicted by the rod of fate.
Then in our line will be born the increaser of the gotra, Aurva by name, of great splendour, with brilliance like fire and sun.
He will bring forth a fire of anger for the destruction of the three worlds, who will reduce the earth with its mountains and forests to ash.
For some time that sage will himself quench that fire, casting it into the mouth of the mare in the ocean.
His son, the greatly fortunate Richika, descendant of Bhrigu, the whole science of the bow will itself come to him, sinless one.
For the ending of the kshatriyas, by a cause joined with fate, he, having received it, will pass it to his son.
In Jamadagni, greatly fortunate, of self purified by austerity, and that tiger of the Bhrigus will bear that Veda.
Having taken Gadhi's daughter, your granddaughter, the great ascetic will beget Rama, a brahmana of kshatriya dharma.
And to your family he will give Vishvamitra, Gadhi's son, a kshatriya doing a brahmin's deeds, like Brihaspati in energy, very righteous, joined with great austerity, greatly radiant one.
Two women will be the cause there in the exchange, grandfather, by command, not otherwise; this will be so.
In the third generation brahminhood will come to you; and you will be a kinsman of the Bhrigus of purified selves."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing the great-souled sage Chyavana's word, King Kushika was glad and said, "So be it," the righteous-souled one, then, best of the Bharatas.
Chyavana of great splendour again urged the king to a boon, and the king said to him:
Very well, I shall take my wish from you, great sage: let my family be Brahman-like, and let its mind be in dharma.
Thus addressed, saying "So be it" in reply, the sage Chyavana, taking leave of the king, went on pilgrimage then.
All this has been told to you by me without remainder, king, the cause of the relationship between the Bhrigus and the Kushikas.
As the sage said, so it came about, king, the birth of Rama and of the sage Vishvamitra.
[Yudhishthira said:] Having gained kingdoms by hundreds and conquered the earth, Bharata, killing men by tens of millions, I am tormented, grandfather.
What will be the state of those fair women who are bereft of husbands, sons, maternal uncles and brothers?
Having killed those elders, relatives and friends, we shall fall head-down into hell, without doubt.
I wish to join my body to fierce austerity, Bharata; I wish here to be instructed in truth, lord of men.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing Yudhishthira's word, the great-minded Bhishma, having examined Yudhishthira carefully with his mind, said:
Hear the secret and wonder that I shall tell you: the goal that is gained by it, Bharata, in the states after death.
By austerity heaven is gained, by austerity fame is gained; long life, abundance and enjoyments are gained by austerity, lord.
Knowledge, realisation, health, beauty, wealth and good fortune are gained by austerity, bull of the Bharatas.
The fruit of non-violence is beauty; of initiation, birth in a family; for eaters of fruit and roots, kingship, and for eaters of leaves, heaven.
One who lives on milk goes to heaven; by bathing one has abundant wealth; by serving the teacher, learning; by constant funeral rites, offspring.
Rich in cows by vegetable initiations, they say heaven is by eating grass; a woman bathing three times a day, drinking air, would gain a sacrifice.
One who bathes daily becomes skilled; a twice-born muttering at both twilights; for one who undertakes the desert, kingship; for one fasting, the vault of heaven.
For those lying on bare ground there are houses and beds; for those in bark and rags, garments and ornaments.
Beds, seats and vehicles for the ascetic joined with yoga; for entering fire, the world of Brahma is ordained.
By restraint of tastes one finds good fortune here; by restraint of meat one's offspring becomes long-lived.
One who lives in the water becomes a king of men; the truthful, best of men, rejoices with the gods.
Fame comes by giving and health by non-violence; by service to a twice-born one gains kingship or abundant twice-bornness.
By giving drinking water, fame is everlasting; by giving food and drink, one is satisfied in desire and enjoyment.
The giver of comfort to all beings is freed from all sorrows; by serving the god one gains kingship and divine form.
By giving the light of a lamp a man becomes sighted; by giving a beautiful sight, one finds memory and wisdom.
By renouncing scent and garlands, abundant fame comes; for those who wear hair and beard, the foremost offspring.
Fasting, initiation and consecration, king, done for twelve years, are better than hero's station.
By giving a daughter to be given to a brahmana, with slave-men and slave-women, ornaments, fields and houses, he gains, best of men.
By sacrifices and fasts one goes to heaven, Bharata; a man who gives offerings and flowers gains a lasting place.
A man who gives a thousand cows adorned with golden horns gains merit in heaven, the world of the gods: so say the troops of divine sages.
He who gives a tawny cow with cloth and a bronze milk-pail with golden-tipped horns, that cow, becoming a wish-granting cow through those qualities, comes to the giver.
As many hairs as a cow has, so much fruit the giver of a cow gains, and he carries across his sons, grandsons and whole family to the seventh generation in the next world.
For one who gives to a brahmana a cow with fee, with golden lovely horns, a bronze milk-pail and a garment of wealth, or a cow of sesame, the worlds of the Vasus are easy to reach.
The gift of cows carries across the next world a man bound by his own deeds and falling into the hell of dense darkness, as a boat with wind carries over a great ocean.
He who gives a daughter to be given to a brahmana, makes a gift of land to a brahmana, and duly gives food, gains the world of Purandara.
The man who gives a dwelling endowed with all qualities to a twice-born joined with study, conduct and virtues also has worlds among the northern Kurus.
By giving oxen, cows and horses a man gains the worlds of the Vasus; they say giving gold leads to heaven, and giving fine gold is better.
By giving an umbrella, the best house; by giving a vehicle and sandals; by giving clothing, fine form; by giving perfume, a man would be fragrant.
One who gives a flower-bearing or fruit-bearing tree to a twice-born, gains a prosperous house full of many jewels and a wife, coming without effort.
The giver of food, drink and juices gains all juices as he wishes; the giver of shelter and covering gains those same, without doubt here.
A man who gives garlands, incense, scents, unguents, baths and wreaths to the twice-born becomes free of disease and handsome in the world of men, king.
One who gives a house not empty of seeds and furnished with beds to a twice-born, delightful with merit and full of many jewels, gains the best foundation, king.
A man who gives a bed to a twice-born, joined with fine scents and varied coverings, gains a wife, beautiful, winged, charming, coming without effort.
A man who lies on a hero's bed becomes a companion of the grandfather, hero; there is nothing higher than that, so say the great sages.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing his words, the descendant of the Kurus, glad in soul, did not like living in a hermitage, desiring the hero's path.
Then Yudhishthira said to the Pandavas, bulls of the Bharatas, "Let what the grandfather said please you."
Then all the Pandavas and the glorious Draupadi honoured Yudhishthira's word, saying "Very well."
[Yudhishthira said:] My curiosity is great there, lord: what gift follows the giver and the given? Tell me.
Go to him, if Brihaspati does not wish to sacrifice for you; Samvarta, pleased, will perform your sacrifice, great king.
I too tell you this: do my word; let the king gain permission; let him not die here in vain.
That river, with the Vrishnis and Andhakas for water, horses for fish, chariots for rafts, the sound of instruments and chariots for its flood, houses for its bathing-places and great crocodiles,
This is Shri herself, Draupadi in form, who took a human state for your sake, unborn, beloved of the worlds, of holy fragrance, Yudhishthira.
